text: What is an ecosystem?
answers: All the living and nonliving things in an area and all their interactions
Only the animals that live in one place
The weather in a region over many years
A single organism and the food it eats
solution: An ecosystem is all the living and nonliving things in an area and all of their interactions. Animals alone, or one organism, are only parts of an ecosystem.
hint: Look for the answer that includes living things, nonliving things, and how they affect each other.

text: What is an organism's environment?
answers: The space, conditions, and all the living and nonliving things around it
Only the other animals of its own kind
The inside of its own body
solution: An environment is the space, conditions, and all the living and nonliving things around one organism. Food and neighbors are only parts of it.
hint: Environment describes everything surrounding one particular organism.

text: A coral reef has fish, sea turtles, coral, salt water, sunlight, and rocks, and they all affect each other. Which word best names the whole reef system?
solution: The reef includes living things (fish, turtles, coral) and nonliving things (salt water, sunlight, rocks) that interact, so it is an ecosystem.
hint: Which word covers living things, nonliving things, and their interactions all together?

text: How is an ecosystem different from an organism’s environment?
answers: An ecosystem is everything in an area and their interactions; an environment is what surrounds one particular organism
They mean exactly the same thing
An environment has only nonliving things; an ecosystem has only living things
An ecosystem is always in the ocean; an environment is always on land
solution: Both include living and nonliving things. An ecosystem describes a whole area and all its interactions. An environment is described from the point of view of one organism: everything around it.
hint: Think about whose point of view each word uses: a whole area, or one organism.

text: Which is the best example of an ecosystem?
answers: A pond where frogs, cattails, insects, water, mud, and sunlight interact
A single frog sitting on a rock
A list of animals that live in Africa
A jar of dry sand with nothing living in it
solution: The pond has living and nonliving parts that affect each other. One frog is an organism, a list is not a place, and dry sand has no living things.
hint: An ecosystem needs living things, nonliving things, and interactions in one area.

text: How big can an ecosystem be?
answers: As small as a puddle or as large as a forest
Only as large as a whole continent
Only big enough to hold trees
solution: An ecosystem can be any size, from a rotting log or puddle to a forest or an ocean, as long as living and nonliving things interact there.
hint: Size does not decide whether something is an ecosystem.

text: For a squirrel in a city park, which list is all part of its environment?
answers: Trees, other squirrels, sidewalks, temperature, and rainwater
Only its own fur and bones
solution: The environment includes everything around the squirrel: living things (trees, squirrels) and nonliving things and conditions (sidewalks, temperature, rain). Its own body is not its environment.
hint: Pick the list with both living and nonliving things around the squirrel.

text: Why does the definition of an ecosystem include “interactions,” not just a list of things?
answers: Because the parts affect one another, and those effects are what make the system work
Because interactions are a kind of nonliving thing
Because a list of things would be too long
solution: An ecosystem is a system: plants use sunlight and water, animals eat plants, decomposers return nutrients. Those connections are what make it an ecosystem, not just a collection of things.
hint: Think about what makes a system more than a pile of parts.

text: The heat, sand, cactus plants, rain, and other animals around a desert tortoise make up the tortoise’s what?
solution: Everything around one organism, living and nonliving, is its environment.
hint: The question describes everything surrounding one organism.

text: A student says, “A tank with only water, gravel, and a lamp is an ecosystem.” What is missing?
answers: Living things that interact with the water, gravel, and light
Nothing, because nonliving things alone make an ecosystem
solution: An ecosystem needs living things interacting with nonliving things. Water, gravel, and light are all nonliving, so the tank is not yet an ecosystem.
hint: Check the definition: living AND nonliving things.

text: The ecosystem vocabulary card shows a reef with sea turtles, fish, and rocks. Why is a reef a good example of an ecosystem?
answers: It has living and nonliving things interacting in one area
solution: A reef has living things (turtles, fish, coral) and nonliving things (rocks, water, sunlight) affecting each other in one area.
hint: Match the picture to the definition of ecosystem.

text: Which of these is a nonliving part of an ecosystem?
solution: Sunlight is nonliving. Mushrooms, deer, and grass are living things: they grow, use energy, and reproduce.
hint: Which one does not grow or reproduce?

text: Which of these is a living part of a pond ecosystem?
solution: Algae are living producers. Water, rocks, and air are nonliving parts of the pond.
hint: Which one grows and makes more of itself?

text: How can you tell a living thing from a nonliving thing?
answers: Living things grow, use energy, and reproduce; nonliving things do not
Living things always move; nonliving things never move
solution: Living things grow, need energy, and reproduce. Movement is not a test: water and wind move, and trees stay in place.
hint: Think about what every living thing does, even a tree.

text: Which list contains only nonliving parts of an ecosystem?
answers: Water, air, soil minerals, and sunlight
Water, fish, soil minerals, and sunlight
solution: Water, air, minerals, and sunlight are nonliving. Fish, grass, bacteria, trees, birds, worms, and mushrooms are living.
hint: Check every item in the list, not just the first one.

text: Which list contains only living things?
answers: Soil minerals, fern, wind, and owl
solution: Bacteria, ferns, owls, and earthworms all grow, use energy, and reproduce. Rocks, rain, wind, sand, salt, water, and light do not.
hint: One nonliving item makes the whole list wrong.

text: A dead log lies on the forest floor. Which statement is accurate?
answers: It is no longer alive, but living things such as fungi and insects use it for food and shelter
It is still living because it is made of wood
It is no longer part of the ecosystem
It is exactly like a rock and was never alive
solution: The log was once alive and is not alive now. It is still part of the ecosystem: decomposers break it down and animals shelter in it.
hint: Think about what happens to a dead log over time.

text: A windstorm belongs in which group of ecosystem parts?
solution: Wind is a nonliving condition of the environment. It can still affect living things, for example by knocking down trees.
hint: Does wind grow or reproduce?

text: Which is an example of a nonliving thing affecting a living thing?
answers: A drought dries up a stream, so fish have less water
A bee carries pollen between flowers
solution: The drought (nonliving) changes the water available to the fish (living). The other choices are living things affecting living things.
hint: Find the choice that starts with something that is not alive.

text: Which is an example of a living thing changing a nonliving part of an ecosystem?
answers: Earthworms tunnel through soil and loosen it
Wind blows sand into a dune
solution: Earthworms (living) change the soil (nonliving). Rain, Sun, rock, wind, and sand are all nonliving.
hint: Which choice begins with a living organism?

text: Which of these is a condition of an environment rather than an organism?
solution: Temperature is a nonliving condition. Rabbits, oak trees, and mold are organisms.
hint: Conditions describe the surroundings, such as how hot or wet it is.

text: Which item in a desert ecosystem is living?
solution: A cactus is a living producer. Sand, heat, and wind are nonliving.
hint: Which one grows and makes seeds?

text: What does “needs” mean in this unit?
answers: Requirements for the well-being of an organism
Things an organism wants for fun
Only the food an organism eats
Only the place an organism sleeps
solution: Needs are requirements for an organism’s well-being: what it must have to stay healthy and survive. Food is one need, not all of them.
hint: Needs are things an organism cannot live well without.

text: Which list names basic needs most animals share?
answers: Food, water, air, and shelter with enough space
solution: Animals need food for energy, water, air (oxygen), and shelter and space to live safely.
hint: Pick the list where every item helps an animal survive.

text: A plant does not eat food. Which needs does a plant have?
answers: Sunlight, water, air, space, and nutrients from the soil
solution: Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide from the air. They also need space and nutrients from the soil.
hint: Think about what a plant uses to make its own food.

text: A pet hamster has food, water, and a cage, but the cage is in a closet that gets very cold at night. Which need is not being met well?
answers: A safe temperature, which is part of good shelter
solution: Food, water, and air are provided. Shelter should protect an animal from harmful conditions like cold, so the cold closet fails that need.
hint: Which need protects an animal from weather and temperature?

text: Why do animals need shelter?
answers: To stay safe from weather and predators and to raise their young
So they never have to move
solution: Shelter, such as a nest, burrow, or den, protects animals from weather and predators and gives them a safe place for young.
hint: Think about what a burrow or nest protects an animal from.

text: Why does an animal need space?
answers: To find enough food, water, and shelter and to move around
Because space is a kind of food
solution: An area that is too small or too crowded may not hold enough food, water, and shelter for every animal.
hint: Space is connected to all the other resources an animal needs.

text: Two deer live in a meadow with plenty of grass, but the only stream dries up. What is most likely to happen?
answers: They must move to find water, or they may not survive
They will be fine because grass is enough
They will start drinking from rocks
solution: Food alone does not meet every need. Without water, the deer must find another water source or they cannot survive.
hint: Is grass enough to meet all of a deer’s needs?

text: Which is a need, not a want, for a person?
solution: Clean water is required for health. The others may be nice to have, but a person can live well without them.
hint: A need is something you cannot live well without.

text: A mushroom breaks down dead leaves on the forest floor. Which need is it meeting?
answers: Its need for food and energy
None, because mushrooms have no needs
solution: Decomposers get their food and energy by breaking down dead material. Mushrooms do not use sunlight to make food.
hint: Decomposers are consumers that eat dead material.

text: In the What Do I Need? game, animals had to collect resources such as food, water, and shelter. Why did some animals not survive a round?
answers: They could not collect enough of the resources they needed
There were more resources than animals
solution: Every animal needs a certain amount of food, water, and shelter. When an animal could not get enough, it did not survive the round.
hint: Think about what “needs” means for survival.

text: Besides water, what important need does a fish get from the water it lives in?
solution: Fish take in oxygen that is dissolved in water using their gills. Air is still a need, even underwater.
hint: What do you take in with every breath that a fish gets from water?

text: In science, what are interactions?
answers: Actions by one thing that have an effect on a different thing
Things that happen only inside one organism
Any two things sitting near each other
solution: An interaction is an action by one thing that affects a different, separate thing, like sunlight warming a lizard or a bee pollinating a flower.
hint: Look for the answer about one thing affecting another.

text: The interactions vocabulary card shows a bowling ball knocking down pins. What idea does it show?
answers: One thing’s action has an effect on another thing
solution: The ball acts and the pins are affected. In an ecosystem, interactions work the same way: one part affects another.
hint: What does the ball do to the pins?

text: Which is an interaction between two living things?
answers: A spider catches a fly in its web
solution: The spider and the fly are both living. The other choices involve only nonliving things.
hint: Both things in the answer must be alive.

text: Which is an interaction between a living thing and a nonliving thing?
answers: A lizard warms itself on a sunny rock
solution: The lizard is living; the rock and sunlight are nonliving. The other choices are two living things.
hint: One part must be alive and the other must not be.

text: Which is an interaction between two nonliving things?
answers: Waves wear away a rocky shore
A beaver cuts down a tree
A deer drinks from a stream
solution: Waves and rock are both nonliving. Beavers, deer, and plant roots are living.
hint: Neither part of the answer can be alive.

text: A beaver builds a dam, and a stream becomes a pond. Which statement best describes what happens?
answers: The beaver changes the water, which changes where fish and plants can live
Nothing else in the ecosystem changes
solution: The beaver (living) changes the water (nonliving), and the new pond changes the homes and food of many other organisms. One interaction can lead to many more.
hint: Follow the effects beyond the beaver itself.

text: Plant roots take in water from the soil. What kind of interaction is this?
answers: A living thing interacting with nonliving things
solution: Roots are part of a living plant. Water and soil are nonliving. The plant takes in water that it needs.
hint: Is the plant living? Are the water and soil living?

text: Which statement about interactions in an ecosystem is accurate?
answers: One change can affect many other parts because the parts are connected
Interactions happen only between animals of the same kind
Nonliving things never affect living things
solution: Ecosystem parts are linked, so a change to one part, such as less rain, can spread to plants, plant eaters, and their predators. Many interactions help organisms.
hint: Think about how a drought could affect more than just water.

text: A cow eats grass. Which kind of interaction is this?
answers: A producer making its own food
solution: The cow is a consumer and grass is a producer. When the cow eats grass, energy passes from the producer to the consumer.
hint: Which one makes food from sunlight, and which one eats?

text: In the Decomposition Race, which was an interaction between living things and nonliving matter?
answers: Earthworms and bacteria broke down the apple and returned matter to the soil
The newspaper was cut into strips
solution: Earthworms and bacteria (living) broke the apple down and returned matter to the soil (nonliving). The other choices do not describe one thing affecting another in the ecosystem.
hint: Which choice has an organism changing something?

text: Mushrooms grow on a dead tree and slowly break it down. What kind of interaction is this?
answers: A decomposer feeding on dead matter and returning nutrients to the soil
A producer making food from sunlight
solution: Mushrooms are decomposers. They get energy from the dead tree and return nutrients to the soil for plants.
hint: What role do mushrooms play in an ecosystem?

text: What does interdependence mean?
answers: The well-being of two or more things is linked together
An animal changes color to hide
Nonliving things melt in the heat
solution: Interdependence means the well-being of two or more things is linked: what happens to one affects the other.
hint: The word contains “depend.” Who depends on whom?

text: The interdependence vocabulary card shows small birds riding on a deer’s back. How could both animals benefit?
answers: The birds eat insects off the deer, so the birds get food and the deer loses pests
The deer carries the birds so they never need to eat
The birds give the deer sunlight
solution: Birds that eat ticks and insects off large animals get food, and the large animal gets rid of pests. Their well-being is linked.
hint: What could a small bird find to eat on a deer?

text: Bees visit flowers for nectar and carry pollen from flower to flower. How are bees and flowering plants interdependent?
answers: Bees get food, and the plants get pollinated so they can make seeds
solution: Bees get nectar and pollen for food. Plants get pollen moved between flowers, which they need to make seeds and fruit. Each helps the other.
hint: What does each one get from the other?

text: If the bees in an area disappeared, what could happen to some flowering plants?
answers: Fewer seeds and fruits could form, so those plants could decrease
Nothing, because plants never depend on animals
The plants would start making honey
solution: Many plants depend on bees for pollination. Without bees, fewer seeds form, so fewer new plants grow.
hint: Think about what bees do for flowers.

text: Which shows that animals depend on plants?
answers: Animals eat plants for energy and use them for shelter
Animals get all of their water from plants
solution: Plants are food for many animals and provide shelter, such as nests in trees.
hint: How do animals use plants every day?

text: Which shows that plants depend on other organisms?
answers: Decomposers return nutrients to the soil that plants use to grow
Animals make soil out of rocks overnight
Plants do not depend on anything
solution: Plants need nutrients from the soil. Decomposers break down dead organisms and return those nutrients, so plants depend on them.
hint: Think about where the nutrients in soil come from.

text: In a meadow, rabbits eat grass and foxes eat rabbits. If a drought kills much of the grass, what will most likely happen to the foxes?
answers: Foxes may decrease too, because there will be fewer rabbits to eat
Foxes will increase because they do not eat grass
Foxes will start making food from sunlight
Foxes will not be affected at all
solution: Foxes depend on rabbits, and rabbits depend on grass. Less grass means fewer rabbits, which means less food for foxes.
hint: Follow the chain from the grass to the foxes.

text: Which sentence uses “interdependence” correctly?
answers: Clownfish and sea anemones show interdependence because each helps the other survive
A rock shows interdependence because it sits alone
Interdependence means an animal eats only one food
Interdependence means nonliving things are alive
solution: A clownfish is protected by the anemone’s stinging tentacles, and the clownfish helps keep the anemone clean and safe. Their well-being is linked.
hint: Look for two things whose well-being is linked.

text: Why do scientists say organisms in an ecosystem are interdependent, even ones that never meet?
answers: Their food and resources are connected through food webs and the environment, so a change to one can reach others
Because they all eat the same food
Because they all share one shelter
solution: An owl may never meet a grasshopper, but owls eat mice that eat grasshoppers’ plants. Connections through food webs and shared resources link them.
hint: Think about indirect connections through a food web.

text: People depend on other organisms for which of these?
answers: Food, oxygen from plants, and materials such as wood and cotton
solution: People eat plants and animals, breathe oxygen that plants release, and use plant materials such as wood and cotton.
hint: Think about what you eat, breathe, and wear.

text: Which human action could break an interdependent link in an ecosystem?
answers: Spraying a chemical that kills the insects birds eat
solution: Killing insects removes food that birds depend on. The other actions support organisms in the ecosystem.
hint: Which action removes something another organism depends on?

text: According to the vocabulary cards, what is a food web?
answers: An interconnected set of food chains
A single straight line of who eats whom
solution: A food web is an interconnected set of food chains. Most organisms eat, and are eaten by, more than one kind of organism.
hint: Food web = many chains connected.

text: Which organism breaks down the remains of dead plants or animals without needing internal digestion?
answers: A decomposer, such as a mushroom
A carnivore, such as a wolf
A herbivore, such as a deer
solution: Decomposers such as mushrooms break down dead remains outside their bodies instead of swallowing and digesting food inside.
hint: This is the definition on the decomposer vocabulary card.

text: Why are decomposers important to an ecosystem?
answers: They break down dead things and return nutrients to the soil for producers
solution: Decomposers recycle matter. Nutrients from dead organisms go back into the soil, where plants use them to grow.
hint: What would happen to dead leaves without them?

text: In an ocean food web like the one on the vocabulary card, which organism is a producer?
solution: Phytoplankton use sunlight to make their own food, so they are the producers. Krill, penguins, and seals are consumers.
hint: Which organism makes food from sunlight?

text: In an ocean food web, krill eat phytoplankton and penguins eat krill. What are penguins?
solution: Penguins get energy by eating other organisms, so they are consumers.
hint: Do penguins make their own food?

text: Why does a food web show an ecosystem more accurately than a single food chain?
answers: Most organisms eat more than one thing and are eaten by more than one thing
Food webs show only nonliving things
solution: Real feeding relationships overlap. A seal eats fish and squid; fish are eaten by seals and birds. A web shows those many links.
hint: Think about how many different foods most animals eat.

text: What would most likely happen to an ecosystem without decomposers?
answers: Dead material would pile up and nutrients would not return to the soil
solution: Without decomposers, dead plants and animals would not break down, and the soil would lose the nutrients plants need.
hint: Decomposers recycle nutrients. What if no one did that job?

text: Where does the energy in an ecosystem’s food web come from first?
solution: Producers capture energy from sunlight to make food. That energy then passes to consumers through the food web.
hint: What do producers use to make food?

text: In an ocean web, seals eat both fish and squid. If the squid population drops, what might seals do?
answers: Eat more fish, which could reduce the fish population
Get energy straight from the Sun
solution: Because seals have more than one food, they may eat more fish when squid are scarce. That can reduce the number of fish, an example of how webs connect.
hint: A food web shows other food choices.

text: Which organism is a producer in a forest ecosystem?
solution: An oak tree makes its own food from sunlight. Squirrels and hawks are consumers, and mushrooms are decomposers.
hint: Which one uses sunlight to make food?

text: Which is the best evidence that a mushroom is a decomposer, not a producer?
answers: It gets energy by breaking down dead material instead of using sunlight
It is shaped like an umbrella
solution: How an organism gets energy decides its role. Mushrooms break down dead material; producers make food from sunlight.
hint: Classify by how it gets energy, not by how it looks.

text: What is a population?
answers: All the organisms of one kind living in an area
Every living and nonliving thing in an area
solution: A population is all the organisms of one kind, such as all the deer, in one area. An ecosystem includes many populations plus nonliving things.
hint: Population = one kind of organism in one place.

text: In the What Do I Need? game, the number of animals grew while the resources stayed the same. What happened to the number of survivors?
solution: The class data showed 6 survivors, then 4, then 3, while the number of animals grew from 6 to 9 to 12.
hint: Look at the survivors column from round 1 to round 3.

text: Why does a bigger population with the same amount of food lead to fewer survivors?
answers: The food is shared among more animals, so some cannot get enough
Food grows faster when there are more animals
solution: Resources are limited. When more animals compete for the same food, water, and shelter, some cannot get enough to survive.
hint: Imagine the same pizza shared by more and more people.

text: What is competition in an ecosystem?
answers: Organisms trying to get the same limited resources
A plant making its own food
solution: Competition happens when organisms need the same resource, such as food, water, or space, and there is not enough for all of them.
hint: Competition happens when there is not enough of something.

text: A meadow has enough food for about 40 rabbits. One spring, 60 rabbits live there. What is most likely to happen?
answers: Some rabbits will not get enough food, so the population will decrease
The meadow will instantly grow extra grass
The rabbits will stop needing food
solution: The meadow cannot support 60 rabbits. Competition for food means some rabbits move away or do not survive, so the population falls.
hint: Compare how many rabbits the meadow can feed with how many live there.

text: Which change would most likely help more animals survive in the game’s ecosystem?
answers: Adding more food, water, and shelter
solution: More resources mean each animal is more likely to get what it needs, so more can survive.
hint: Survival depends on resources per animal.

text: Which resources do animals in a population compete for?
solution: Animals compete for the things they need: food, water, shelter, and space.
hint: Think back to the list of needs.

text: A pond has a big increase in frogs. What could happen to the insects the frogs eat?
answers: The insect population may decrease because more frogs are eating them
Nothing, because frogs and insects are not connected
solution: More predators eat more prey, so the insect population is likely to go down.
hint: More frogs means more insects get eaten.

text: After the insect population falls, what could happen to the large frog population?
answers: Some frogs may not survive because there is less food, so the frog population could decrease
The frogs will keep increasing forever
The frogs will switch to making their own food
The frogs will not be affected
solution: With fewer insects, frogs compete for less food. Some do not survive, so the frog population can shrink. Populations rise and fall together.
hint: What do the frogs need that is now scarce?

text: Plants compete too. What do crowded plants compete for?
solution: Plants need sunlight, water, space for roots and leaves, and soil nutrients. Crowded plants must share these.
hint: What does a plant need to make food and grow?

text: Which statement best describes the relationship between population size and survival when resources are limited?
answers: As the population increases, each animal’s share of resources decreases, so a smaller fraction survives
Survival depends only on the weather
solution: With limited resources, more animals means less for each one. In the class data, 6 of 6 survived in round 1 but only 3 of 12 in round 3.
hint: Think about the share of resources each animal gets.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. How many animals survived round 1?
solution: Round 1 shows 6 survivors and 0 animals that did not survive.
hint: Read the survived number for round 1.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. How many animals played in round 2?
solution: Add the survivors and the animals that did not survive: 4 + 5 = 9 animals.
hint: Total animals = survived + did not survive.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. How many animals played in round 3?
solution: 3 survived and 9 did not, so 3 + 9 = 12 animals played.
hint: Add both columns for round 3.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. Which round had the most animals that did not survive?
solution: Round 3 had 9 animals that did not survive, more than round 2 (5) or round 1 (0).
hint: Compare the “did not survive” column.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. What pattern does the data show?
answers: As the number of animals increased, the number of survivors decreased
As the number of animals increased, more animals survived
The number of survivors stayed the same
solution: Animals increased from 6 to 9 to 12, while survivors decreased from 6 to 4 to 3.
hint: Find the total each round, then compare with the survivors.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. What fraction of the animals survived in round 3?
answers: 12 out of 12, or all of them
solution: Round 3 had 3 + 9 = 12 animals, and 3 survived. 3/12 = 1/4. Be careful: 9 is the number that did not survive, not the total.
hint: First find the total number of animals in round 3.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. How did the total number of animals change from round to round?
solution: Totals: round 1 is 6 + 0 = 6, round 2 is 4 + 5 = 9, round 3 is 3 + 9 = 12. The population grew by 3 each round.
hint: Add the two columns for each round.

text: A student answered “How was each round different?” with “Each round had a different amount of survivors.” What would make this answer stronger?
answers: Adding the numbers and a reason: survivors fell from 6 to 4 to 3 as the population grew while resources stayed the same
solution: A strong answer describes the change with data and explains it: the population grew (6, 9, 12), resources did not, so survivors dropped (6, 4, 3).
hint: Strong answers include data and a reason.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. If a fourth round had 15 animals with the same resources, which result is most likely?
answers: About 3 or fewer survive, and more animals do not survive than in round 3
More animals survive than in round 1
The number of animals that do not survive drops to 0
solution: The pattern shows survivors falling and losses rising as the population grows. With 15 animals and the same resources, losses would most likely grow again.
hint: Continue the pattern in both columns.

text: Class data from What Do I Need?: Round 1: 6 survived, 0 did not. Round 2: 4 survived, 5 did not. Round 3: 3 survived, 9 did not. In round 2, about what fraction of the animals did not survive?
answers: 5 out of 9, a little more than half
4 out of 9, a little less than half
solution: Round 2 had 4 + 5 = 9 animals, and 5 did not survive. 5/9 is a little more than half.
hint: Use the round 2 total as the denominator.

text: In the What Do I Need? activity, what changed from round to round?
answers: The amount of food, water, and shelter
solution: The population grew each round (6, 9, 12) while the resources stayed the same, so the activity tested how population size affects survival.
hint: Look at how the totals changed.

text: A wildfire burns most of the grass on a prairie. What happens first to the animals that eat grass?
answers: They have less food, so some move away or do not survive
solution: Grass is their food. When it burns, herbivores must find food elsewhere or they may not survive.
hint: What did those animals depend on?

text: A new pond forms after heavy rains. What is most likely to happen?
answers: Animals that need water move in, and some populations grow
solution: A new water source meets a need for many organisms, so animals and plants that need water can move in and grow.
hint: Water is a basic need. What happens when more is available?

text: People build a parking lot on a field. How does this most likely affect the ecosystem?
answers: Habitat and food are lost, so some organisms must move or may not survive
Plants grow better on the pavement
solution: Pavement removes plants, soil, and shelter. Organisms that lived there lose food and homes.
hint: What did the field provide that pavement does not?

text: Wolves are removed from an area, and the deer population grows very large. What will most likely happen to the plants deer eat?
answers: The plants will be overeaten and decrease
Nothing will happen to the plants
solution: Wolves kept the deer population in check. With more deer eating, plants are eaten faster than they can grow back.
hint: Follow the effect from wolves to deer to plants.

text: Which is a nonliving change that could affect an ecosystem?
answers: A new kind of insect arriving
solution: A drought is a change in a nonliving factor (water). The other choices are changes in living things.
hint: Which choice is about weather or water, not organisms?

text: Which is a living change that could affect an ecosystem?
answers: A new species that eats native plants moves in
solution: A new species is a living change. Floods, temperature, and eruptions are nonliving.
hint: Which choice is about an organism?

text: After a flood, nutrient-rich mud is left on a riverbank. Over the next season, what is most likely?
answers: Plants grow well there, providing food for consumers
No plants can ever grow there again
The mud instantly turns into rock
solution: Nutrients help producers grow, and more plants mean more food for consumers. Not every change is harmful.
hint: What do nutrients do for plants?

text: Why can a change to one population affect many others?
answers: Organisms are connected through food webs and shared resources
Every organism eats the same food
solution: Because organisms are interdependent, a change in one population changes the food or competition for others.
hint: Think about food webs and interdependence.

text: Farmers spray a chemical that kills many insects. What could happen to birds that eat insects?
answers: The birds may have less food, and their population may decrease
The birds will have more food
The birds will start eating the chemical
The birds are not connected to insects
solution: Insects are the birds’ food. Fewer insects means less food, so the bird population may drop.
hint: What do those birds depend on?

text: Students plant native flowers in a schoolyard. Which effect is most likely?
answers: More pollinators such as bees and butterflies visit, which helps other plants make seeds
solution: Flowers provide nectar and pollen. More pollinators visit, and their pollination helps other plants reproduce.
hint: Who depends on flowers for food?

text: Which change would most likely help a population of fish in a stream?
answers: Cleaning up pollution so the water is healthier
Damming the stream until it dries up
solution: Fish need clean water with oxygen. Removing pollution improves their environment; the other changes harm it.
hint: Which choice improves a need fish have?

text: In the Zoo Tour activity, what must a strong solution do for its animal?
answers: Meet all of the animal’s needs and solve the problems
Hold as many visitors as possible
solution: The Expert level of the rubric says the solution addressed the animal’s needs and solved all the problems.
hint: Check the Solution row of the rubric.

text: A zoo is designing a home for a polar bear. Which feature best meets its needs?
answers: Cold water for swimming, space to roam, and a den for shelter
A tiny cage with no water
A tank of warm water only
solution: Polar bears live in cold Arctic environments, swim in icy water, and use dens. A good habitat copies those conditions.
hint: Think about where polar bears live in nature.

text: What should a desert tortoise enclosure include?
answers: Warm, dry areas, shade or burrows, and plants it can eat
A dark room with no plants
solution: Desert tortoises need warmth, places to escape the heat, and plants to eat, like their natural desert environment.
hint: Match the habitat to a desert.

text: A team designs a monkey habitat with food, water, and climbing branches but no shaded or sheltered area. What should they add?
answers: Shelter or shade so the monkeys can rest and stay safe from the weather
solution: Food, water, and space for climbing are met, but shelter is a basic need too. Adding shade or shelter completes the solution.
hint: Check the list of needs: food, water, shelter, space.

text: According to the Zoo Tour rubric, what makes a presentation Expert?
answers: All members take part, stay on topic, are prepared, and finish in 3 minutes or less
solution: The Expert presentation level describes full participation, staying on topic, eye contact, preparation, enthusiasm, a 3-minute limit, and listening to other teams.
hint: Look at the Presentation row, Expert column.

text: Which row of the Zoo Tour rubric checks whether the solution meets the animal’s needs?
solution: The Solution row scores how well the design addressed the animal’s needs and solved the problems.
hint: Which row talks about the animal’s needs?

text: Why should a zoo habitat be planned around the animal’s natural environment?
answers: The animal’s body and behavior suit those conditions, so copying them helps it meet its needs
Zoo animals do not have needs
It always makes the zoo cheaper
solution: Animals are suited to their natural environments. Matching temperature, water, food, and shelter helps a zoo animal stay healthy.
hint: Why would a polar bear struggle in a desert?

text: A team gives a penguin a pool but forgets any dry area. What problem does the design still have?
answers: Penguins also need dry land to rest and nest, not just water
Pools are nonliving, so they are not allowed
solution: Penguins swim to hunt but rest, molt, and nest on land or ice. A habitat needs both.
hint: Do penguins spend all their time in water?

text: What is the best first step for designing an animal’s habitat?
answers: Research the animal’s needs: food, water, shelter, space, and climate
solution: Engineers start by understanding the problem. Here that means learning exactly what the animal needs.
hint: Start by finding out what the animal requires.

text: Which behavior shows Expert teamwork on the Zoo Tour rubric?
answers: Showing respect, listening, sharing ideas, and actively participating
Letting one person do all the work
Not getting along on many occasions
Needing several reminders to stay on task
solution: The Expert teamwork level describes respect, good listening, sharing ideas, collaborating, celebrating, and active participation.
hint: Look at the Teamwork row, Expert column.

text: A frog habitat has a pond and plants, but the pond is filled with untreated tap water containing chlorine. Why is this a problem?
answers: Frogs need clean water, and chemicals can harm them through their skin
The plants make the chlorine safe instantly
solution: Frogs take in water through their thin skin, so chemicals like chlorine can harm them. Their water need is for clean water.
hint: How do frogs take in water?

text: In a claim–evidence–reasoning answer, what is the claim?
answers: A statement that answers the question
The science idea that explains why
solution: The claim is your answer to the question. Evidence supports it with data, and reasoning explains why the evidence supports it.
hint: The claim comes first and answers the prompt.

text: What counts as evidence in a claim–evidence–reasoning answer?
answers: Observations and data that support the claim
solution: Evidence is what you observed or measured, such as the number of survivors each round.
hint: Evidence is something you can point to in your data.

text: What does reasoning do in a claim–evidence–reasoning answer?
answers: Connects the evidence to the claim using a science idea
Repeats the claim in new words
Gives the date of the activity
solution: Reasoning explains WHY the evidence supports the claim, using a science idea such as limited resources and competition.
hint: Reasoning answers “why does this evidence prove my claim?”

text: Prompt: Describe the relationship between population size and survival. Which is the best claim?
answers: When a population grows and resources stay the same, fewer individuals survive
solution: A claim directly answers the prompt by stating the relationship. The other choices do not describe a relationship.
hint: A claim answers the prompt in one clear sentence.

text: Which is the best evidence for the claim that larger populations have fewer survivors when resources are limited?
answers: In round 1 all 6 animals survived, but in round 3 only 3 of 12 animals survived
The more people there were, the harder it was
We played a game in class
solution: Strong evidence is specific data from the investigation. The first choice compares rounds with numbers; the others are general statements.
hint: Look for numbers from the activity.

text: Which is the best reasoning for that claim?
answers: Resources like food are limited, so when more animals share them, some cannot get enough to survive
We did Explore 2 and saw it happen
The more people, the fewer survivors
solution: Reasoning uses a science idea, limited resources and competition, to explain why bigger populations had fewer survivors.
hint: Reasoning explains WHY using a science idea, not just what happened.

text: A student’s reasoning says, “We did Explore 2, and the more people there were, the fewer survivors.” What is missing?
answers: The science idea of limited resources and competition that explains why
solution: That sentence restates what happened. Reasoning must explain why: resources were limited, so more animals competing meant some could not get enough.
hint: Does the sentence explain WHY?

text: In the Decomposition Race, a student wrote, “There was mold on the apples.” Is this a claim, evidence, or reasoning?
solution: An observation of mold is evidence: something seen during the investigation.
hint: Was this something observed?

text: Which sentence is reasoning, not evidence?
answers: Animals that cannot get enough food and water cannot survive, so a larger population with the same resources has fewer survivors
Round 3 had 9 animals that did not survive
solution: The first sentence uses a science idea to explain the pattern. The others are data points, which are evidence.
hint: Data points are evidence. Which one explains a cause?

text: Why should evidence include numbers when you have them?
answers: Numbers make the evidence specific and easy to check
Numbers replace the need for a claim
solution: Specific data, like “3 of 12 survived,” shows exactly what happened and lets others check it.
hint: Compare “fewer survived” with “3 of 12 survived.”

text: A student wrote as evidence: “When the population of a nation increases, there is less food for everyone.” Why is this weak evidence for the class activity?
answers: It is a general idea, not data from the activity; it fits better as reasoning
It is a claim about plants
solution: Evidence should come from the investigation, such as survivor counts. A general statement about limited food is a science idea, which belongs in reasoning.
hint: Did this come from the class data?

text: Claim: Living and nonliving things interact in an ecosystem. Which is the best supporting evidence?
answers: Plants take in water from the soil and use sunlight to make food
solution: Plants (living) use water, soil, and sunlight (nonliving), so this shows living and nonliving things interacting. The others do not describe a living–nonliving interaction.
hint: Find a living thing using something nonliving.

text: Claim: Living and nonliving things interact in an ecosystem. Which evidence supports the claim?
answers: Fish get oxygen from the water they live in
solution: Fish (living) take in oxygen dissolved in water (nonliving). Fins and egg laying are traits; two fish swimming together is living–living.
hint: Which choice links a living thing and a nonliving thing?

text: Claim: Living and nonliving things interact in an ecosystem. Which evidence does NOT support this claim?
answers: Earthworms mix and loosen the soil
A lizard warms itself on a sunny rock
Tree roots break apart a rock
solution: A hawk eating a mouse is two living things interacting. It is a real interaction, but it does not support a claim about living and nonliving things.
hint: Look for the example with no nonliving part.

text: A student’s evidence says, “All organisms need water to survive.” How could it connect to the claim more clearly?
answers: Explain that organisms take in water, a nonliving thing, from their environment
solution: Naming the interaction, organisms taking water from their environment, ties the fact directly to the claim about living and nonliving things.
hint: Say how the need for water is an interaction.

text: Which is an example of a nonliving thing affecting living things?
answers: Cold winter temperatures cause some animals to hibernate
solution: Temperature (nonliving) changes animal behavior (living). The other choices are living–living interactions.
hint: Which choice starts with a condition like temperature?

text: Which is an example of living things affecting nonliving things?
answers: A beaver dam changes the flow of a stream
solution: Beavers (living) change the stream (nonliving). The other choices are nonliving–nonliving.
hint: Which choice has an organism causing the change?

text: Living things rely on their ecosystem to survive. Which example shows this?
answers: A bird builds a nest from twigs and grass in a tree
solution: The bird uses materials from its ecosystem for shelter. The others involve no living things.
hint: Which example shows an organism using its surroundings?

text: How does the Decomposition Race support the claim that living and nonliving things interact?
answers: Earthworms and bacteria broke down the apple and returned matter to the soil
The apple was cut in half
solution: Living worms and bacteria changed the apple and the soil. That is evidence of living things interacting with nonliving matter.
hint: Which choice shows organisms changing something?

text: Why does the claim organizer ask for four pieces of evidence instead of one?
answers: Several pieces of evidence make a claim stronger and more convincing
One piece of evidence is always wrong
solution: More independent examples show the claim holds in many situations, which makes it more convincing.
hint: Is a claim stronger with one example or many?

text: Which set of four pieces of evidence best supports the claim that living and nonliving things interact?
answers: Plants use sunlight; animals breathe air; fish live in water; worms loosen soil
Hawks eat mice; foxes eat rabbits; owls eat voles; snakes eat frogs
Rocks are hard; water is wet; sand is dry; air is clear
Dogs bark; cats meow; birds sing; frogs croak
solution: Each example in the first set links a living thing with a nonliving thing. The second set is living–living, the third is only nonliving, and the fourth describes animal sounds.
hint: Every piece should pair something living with something nonliving.

text: Which nonliving thing does almost every organism interact with?
solution: Nearly every organism needs water. Mushrooms, hawks, and grass are living things.
hint: Which choice is nonliving?
